segments.title: Passion as a guide and a source of bias
segments.body: Passion can be a strong reason to study history, but it can also harden into bias and make a researcher see more in the sources than they contain. Tracing a family's military service was one route into naval history. Roughly 100 relatives went to World War I and roughly 120 went to World War II. They fought for Britain, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, South Africa, the United States and, in one distant relative's case, France. Many were drawn to dangerous work involving fighter aircraft, commando operations, destroyers, or submarines, and many died. Tracking down their histories became a lasting passion.

evidence.note: Passion can guide historical study or bias it, and family service in both world wars prompted an interest in naval history.

segments.summary: A personal connection can make historical research compelling, but it can also steer a researcher toward a preferred reading of the evidence.

segments.title: Uncle Sid and the limits of wartime blame
segments.body: Sid was a Fleet Air Arm fighter pilot travelling through the Indian Ocean to join his squadron when a German surface raider sank his ship. The admiral in charge of the area organized ships to hunt the raider, but his choice proved wrong. He had acted on the best information available because his superiors had not passed on everything he needed. After the ship's gun crew were killed, Sid and his best friend took over the weapon and kept firing while others escaped in lifeboats. The family does not know where Sid's best friend ended up. Sid's body washed ashore in India and was buried somewhere along the coast. Dr. Clarke hopes to find the grave, visit it, and pay his family's respects. Sid was remembered secondhand as "rip roaring fun." His sister lost all three of her brothers, so her daughters grew up without uncles. In this personal interpretation, the admiral was not responsible because he did the best he could with the information available, while the causes ran up and down the chain of command.

evidence.note: Sid's journey to join a Fleet Air Arm squadron and death in an Indian Ocean sinking, including the failed German raider hunt, incomplete information from higher command, his work on the ship's gun during the evacuation, and the judgment that the admiral was not responsible.
Sid is remembered secondhand as "rip roaring fun," and his sister's loss of all three brothers left her daughters without uncles.

segments.summary: In this personal account, the admiral was not responsible for a family loss at sea: he acted on incomplete information, and the causes ran through the wider chain of command.
